rubric: DISCRETE MATHEMATICS / THE LANGUAGE OF MATHEMATICS / CHAPTER 2

slides.title: Relations and functions
slides.main: Mathematics describes data schemas and module interfaces with one vocabulary.

captions: Relations and functions: two words you use every day
Every database is full of relations: an order is linked to a customer, a post to an author
Every module is full of functions: a value goes in, exactly one comes out
Mathematics describes both with one vocabulary — pairs, relations, functions

body.text: An order is linked to a customer, a post to an author, a comment to a post: every database of yours is full of relations, every module is full of functions.

slides.title: Ordered pair
slides.main: Swap the elements and you get a different pair: order is the essence of the thing here.

captions: In a set order played no role: {1, 2} = {2, 1}
In a pair order is the essence: the first and second elements occupy different positions
A point on a map is a pair (latitude, longitude); swap them and you get a different place
In code this is a tuple or a two-element array in which position carries meaning

body.text: In code you store such things as tuples and two-element arrays where position carries meaning — and that is all the mathematics of a pair.

slides.title: Cartesian product
slides.sub: All possible pairs of two sets
slides.main: The Cartesian product is the groundwork for the product rule, on which combinatorics rests.

captions: Take two sets: three T-shirts and two pairs of trousers
All possible pairs are the Cartesian product: six outfits
This is the groundwork for the product rule: 3 · 2 = 6 — the basis of combinatorics
In databases this corresponds to the cross join of tables

body.text: In databases it is the cross join of tables — the one that, with no filtering condition, produces all combinations of rows.

slides.title: Relation
slides.sub: A subset of the Cartesian product
slides.main: A table in a database is a relation — hence the word "relational".

captions: A relation is a subset of the Cartesian product: some pairs are marked as related
"An order belongs to a customer" is the pairs (order, customer); in a database it is a foreign key
"Is friends with" is pairs of people, symmetric by meaning: both halves are marked
A table in a database is a relation — hence the word "relational"

frames.text: a table row = a pair of the relation

body.text: The whole theory of relational databases is the theory of relations.

slides.title: Reflexivity
slides.main: Reflexivity is checked on one element: is it related to itself.

captions: Reflexivity: every element is related to itself — the whole diagonal is marked
"Equals" is reflexive: any number equals itself
"Less than" is not reflexive: a number is not less than itself
In a data schema: an employee can refer to themselves through the manager

body.text: An employees table that refers to itself through a manager calmly allows records where both halves of the pair point to the same row.

slides.title: Symmetry
slides.sub: If the first is related to the second, then vice versa
slides.main: The difference between friendship and a subscription instantly turns into a data-schema check.

captions: Symmetry: if the first is related to the second, then the second is related to the first
Friendship is symmetric: both became friends — a link in both directions
A subscription is not symmetric: you follow an author, but the author does not follow you
In a schema: friendship is stored as a pair in both directions, a subscription — in one only

frames.text: a R b ⇒ b R a
a ↔ b: both halves of the pair

body.text: In a friendship table the pairs go in both directions or the lookup goes both ways; in a subscriptions table — in one only.

slides.title: Transitivity
slides.sub: Through a third — to a new conclusion
slides.main: If the first is related to the second, and the second to the third, then the first is related to the third.

captions: Transitivity: the first is related to the second, the second to the third — so the first to the third
"Is an ancestor of" is transitive: an ancestor of an ancestor is also an ancestor
"Knows" is not transitive: a friend of your friend is not necessarily a friend; the network merely recommends
In package managers: a dependency of a dependency is your dependency

frames.text: a R b, b R c ⇒ a R c
know each other? — does not follow
the network shows them as a recommendation
app depends on lib-c as well (transitively)
direct dependencies are solid, transitive — dashed

body.text: A dependency of a dependency is your dependency: in package managers this whole chain is called exactly that — transitive dependencies.

slides.title: Equivalence
slides.main: An equivalence cuts a set into non-overlapping classes: inside a class everything is considered identical.

captions: Reflexivity + symmetry + transitivity — an equivalence relation
"The same remainder when divided by 3" is an equivalence; the color shows the remainder
An equivalence cuts a set into non-overlapping classes
Grouping by a key is a partition into classes; the result of GROUP BY is ready-made classes

frames.text: a ~ b, b ~ c ⇒ a ~ c
GROUP BY n % 3  →  3 classes of 3 elements

body.text: Grouping by a key in your favorite language is exactly a partition into equivalence classes; the result of grouping by a field in a database is ready-made classes.

slides.title: Partial order
slides.main: "Partial" is the key word: there are elements that cannot be compared with each other at all.

captions: Reflexivity + antisymmetry + transitivity — a partial order, like "≤"
"Partial": there are elements that cannot be compared — 2 and 3 do not divide each other
In a dependency tree, packages from different branches are not ordered relative to each other
Topological sorting stretches a partial order into a build line

frames.text: utils and net are not ordered relative to each other
build order: core → utils → net → app

body.text: When you need to stretch the order into a line, topological sorting works — it assembles a partial order into a sequence.

slides.title: A function as a contract
slides.sub: Exactly one image for each input
slides.main: A mathematical function cannot crash and cannot return different results for the same inputs.

captions: Now functions: a relation that has an additional contract
Every element of the domain has exactly one image in the codomain
Two answers for one input or an input with no answer is no longer a function
A signature in a language is the same contract written in types: a string goes in, a number comes out
A mathematical function does not crash and gives the same output for the same input

frames.text: exactly one arrow from each input
a has two answers, c has none
one input — always the same output, no exceptions

body.text: A function signature in a programming language is the same contract written in types: a string goes in, a number comes out.

slides.title: Injection, surjection, bijection
slides.sub: How a function fills the output
slides.main: A bijection is precisely an invertible function; encoding and decoding live exactly on bijections.

captions: Functions are distinguished by how they fill the output
Injection: different inputs give different outputs — nothing is glued together, but places may be left over
Surjection: every element of the output is occupied — no empty places, but inputs may be glued together
Bijection — both at once: one to one, and the function can be turned around
Inverse function: encoding and decoding live on bijections

frames.text: number 3 goes to nobody, but nothing is glued
all numbers are occupied, but a and b are glued
f⁻¹: arrows in the opposite direction

body.text: Seating guests so that no free chairs are left is a surjection; a function can be turned back only if it is a bijection.

slides.title: Pure function
slides.main: The result depends only on the arguments — the same input always gives the same output.

captions: A pure function in programming is a mathematical function by construction
It does not look at the time, does not read global variables, does not write to a database
Tests love it for that: one input — one expected output, no mocks
Memoization saves input–output pairs: a table of correspondences is a relation

frames.text: the result depends only on the arguments
no hidden inputs and no side effects
no mocks and no environment setup
a table of pairs is a relation

body.text: A table of pairs, if you remember, is a relation — memoization takes us back to the beginning of the chapter.

slides.title: Summary
slides.main: Foreign keys, grouping, topological sorting and pure functions — in one vocabulary.

captions: Summing up the chapter
Pairs gather into a Cartesian product; a subset of the product is a relation
Reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity divide relations into equivalences and orders
A function is a relation with the contract "exactly one output"; its kinds are injection, surjection, bijection
Foreign keys, grouping, topological sorting, pure functions — one vocabulary
Next — the calculator: combinatorics will teach us to count how many there are in total

frames.text: Chapter 3 · combinatorics: how many there are →

body.text: The next chapter is the calculator: combinatorics will teach us to count how many there are in total, from PIN codes to poker hands.
